title: Influence of CO<sub>2</sub>/CH<sub>4</sub> production ratios on the isotope signature of methane
content:
by M. Elizabeth Holmes, Alexis E. Slentz, Samantha H. Bosman, Yueh-Fen Li, Rachel M. Wilson, Apryl L. Perry, Ruth K. Varner, Scott R. Saleska, Virginia I. Rich, Suzanne B. Hodgkins, Derek A. Smith, Sarah C. Bagby, EMERGE Field Team , EMERGE Institute Coordinators , Jeffrey P. Chanton

Stable carbon isotopes are often used to infer dominant methanogenic pathways in wetland ecosystems. We performed closed system incubations with Sphagnum bog peat, monitoring CO2 and CH4 production and isotopic composition across incubation temperatures and over time. We observed higher CO2 production relative to CH4 production (CO2/CH4 > 1). Whereas for closed methanogenic systems one would typically expect the CO2 pool and resultant CH4 to become increasingly enriched as 13C-depleted carbon is transformed to CH4, we saw the stable carbon isotopic composition of both gases became increasingly 13C-depleted in parallel over the course of the incubations. We hypothesized that these unusual trends were due to CO2 with organic matter isotopic composition (‑25 ‰) being added by non-fractionating catabolic processes at a higher rate than CO2 reduction to CH4, resulting in increasing 13C depletion in the CO2 pool over time. Methane was formed from that increasingly depleted CO2 pool at a relatively constant apparent fractionation factor and thus its δ13C became more depleted over time as well. We developed an explanatory mass balance model which reproduced our observations and was consistent with our hypothesis. The isotope mass balance model accurately reproduced changes in δ13C-CO2 and δ13C-CH4 under conditions consistent with hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis drawing from a progressively 13C-depleted CO2 pool. These results show the CO2/CH4 production ratio strongly influences δ13C-CH4 by controlling the δ13C-CO2. Small shifts in CO2-dominated versus CH4-dominated metabolism can substantially alter δ13C-CH4 even in the absence of major changes in methanogenic pathway, potentially leading to misinterpretation of isotope signals from incubations, porewaters, or emissions if not considered.
